summary: Improves IPv6 Duplicate Address Detection so it can reliably tell when a node's own probe has been looped back to it, a case that otherwise causes false duplicate-address failures. It lets a node recognize its own probe and avoid wrongly giving up an address. It builds on RFC 4862.

plainLanguage.summary: Before using a name tag, you shout the name to see if anyone else has it. Sometimes your own echo comes back and fools you. This adds a trick to recognize your own echo.

questions: how does the dad nonce work
subtitle: A random nonce lets an IPv6 node recognize its own duplicate address probe when the network loops it back.

tldr.problem: If a node's own Duplicate Address Detection probe is looped back to it, for example by a circuit loopback test, the node wrongly concludes the address is a duplicate and IPv6 stays down until someone intervenes manually.
tldr.mechanism: The sender puts a random nonce in the Nonce option of each DAD Neighbor Solicitation and remembers it. A received DAD message with a matching stored nonce is its own looped back probe, so it is logged and dropped.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 can self-heal after a loopback is placed and removed. The RFC updates RFCs 4429, 4861 and 4862.

facts.label: Mechanism
facts.value: Random single-use nonce in the Nonce option

today: RFC 7527 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 4429, RFC 4861 and RFC 4862.

sections.title: Looped Back DAD Probes
sections.content:
Appendix A of RFC 4862 discusses IPv6 loopback suppression and Duplicate Address Detection (DAD), and mentions a hardware-assisted way to detect looped back DAD messages. If hardware cannot suppress them, a software solution is needed. This RFC specifies one, called Enhanced DAD.

Its focus is a Neighbor Solicitation (NS) looped back to the interface that sent it during DAD. Detecting a looped back Neighbor Advertisement does not solve the problem, and other looped back ND messages are out of scope. The RFC also covers Optimistic DAD (RFC 4429), which can fail for the same reason.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the message you send out to check a name is bounced straight back to you. Enhanced DAD teaches the sender to notice that.

sections.title: The Problem Service Providers Reported
sections.content:
In the first scenario, a circuit connected to an IPv6-enabled router interface is being loopback tested. The interface sends an NS for its link-local address DAD, the circuit reflects it back, and the interface enters a DAD-failed state. After the loopback is removed IPv4 returns to operation, but IPv6 stays in DAD-failed state until manual intervention.

In the second scenario, two broadband modems from the same provider terminate on the same Layer 3 interface of an access concentrator and share a local network. The NS reaches one modem, which puts it on the local network, and the second modem forwards it back to the concentrator. That interface typically serves thousands of modems, and all of them lose IPv6 until the state is cleared.

The problem is not limited to link-local addresses; it exists for any IPv6 address type, including global addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A test on a cable can bounce your shout straight back, and one echo can knock out thousands of customers at once.

sections.title: Mitigations That Need No Code Change
sections.content:
Two options need no change to existing implementations. One is to disable DAD on an interface. It is the simplest, but it needs care on point-to-point interfaces, is a one-time manual setting on each interface, and means genuine duplicates on the link will not be detected. A service provider router SHOULD support turning DAD off per interface.

The other is to use the Layer 2 protocol. Some protocols can detect a loopback, for example PPP with its magic number (RFC 1661). When one does, the device MUST temporarily disable DAD on the interface and MUST re-enable it when the loopback goes away or the interface state changes. This should be enabled by default and MUST be configurable where the Layer 2 technology can detect loopbacks. It needs no extra state or timer.

Neither option needs both ends to support it, and they work for a unidirectional loopback. They may not work for a bidirectional loopback, because a device that does not follow a mitigation will still disable IPv6 on that interface.
sections.plainLanguage: You can either stop shouting altogether, which means you miss real clashes, or let the cable tell you when it is in test mode.

sections.title: The Enhanced DAD Algorithm
sections.content:
The algorithm uses a random number in the Nonce option from SEcure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971); pseudorandom functions are covered in RFC 4086. Each NS(DAD) for each address of an interface uses a different nonce.

Senders. A node configured for Enhanced DAD MUST generate a random nonce for each NS(DAD) on a tentative or optimistic address, MUST store it, and MUST include it in the Nonce option. If no failure shows up within RetransTimer milliseconds after DupAddrDetectTransmits solicitations, the address moves to the assigned state. If a probe is looped back, the interface sends another MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT NS(DAD) messages, RetransTimer milliseconds apart, each with a new nonce. If none is looped back, probing stops, which MAY also be done manually, and the address moves to assigned.

Receivers. On receiving an NS(DAD) whose Target Address matches its own tentative or optimistic address, the node compares the nonce with its stored nonces. On a match it SHOULD log a system management message, SHOULD update a statistics counter, and MUST drop the message. If there is a nonce but no match, it SHOULD log a DAD-failed message and update the counter.

Two nodes using the same Target Address and the same random nonce would be wrongly treated as a loopback. The RFC notes this is logged, and because the nodes keep probing it is unlikely they pick the same nonce twice. The algorithm could detect any looped back ND message, but it is not recommended outside DAD because of the extra state.
sections.plainLanguage: You put a secret code on each shout and remember it. When a shout comes back with your own code, you know it is your echo and ignore it. A shout with a different code is a real clash.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 4861 and Genuine Duplicates
sections.content:
The RFC appends text to the Source Address definition in Section 4.3 of RFC 4861: a node configured for Enhanced DAD adds the Nonce option to an NS with an unspecified source address and implements the Enhanced DAD state machine. It also adds that RetransTimer MAY be overridden by a link-specific document if a node supports Enhanced DAD.

The nonce also helps spot genuine duplicates on networks that can loop messages. The node then follows the manual intervention of Section 5.4.5 of RFC 4862. In networks where a trusted router serves untrusted hosts, such as cable broadband with an access concentrator that proxies DAD, the concentrator SHOULD log a message, drop the received ND message, and block the modem on whose Layer 2 service identifier the duplicate NS(DAD) or NA arrived. Other networks with the same trust model MAY do the same.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone really does have your name tag, the code helps you notice. In some networks the boss can then cut off the one who copied it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it neither improves nor reduces the security posture of RFC 4862. A rogue node can deliberately change the nonce to defeat the looped back detection, and the nonce does not protect against a denial of service in which a rogue replies with a fake NA to every DAD probe. Disabling DAD has an obvious security issue too. In each case SEND is recommended, and Source Address Validation Improvement (RFC 6620) also protects against on-link rogues.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster can still fiddle with the code or send fake answers, so the RFC points to stronger protection for networks that need it.
